# MOVEit Transfer / CL0P Mass Exploitation: Investigation Report

## Executive Summary

CVE-2023-34362 was a critical, unauthenticated SQL-injection vulnerability in Progress MOVEit Transfer, a secure managed file-transfer platform. The vulnerability enabled remote attackers to access the MOVEit database and, depending on the database engine, infer database contents or execute SQL statements capable of altering or deleting database elements. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) assigns the vulnerability a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8, categorized as Critical, with the vector `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)).

The evidence indicates that exploitation began before public disclosure. Mandiant reported that the earliest evidence identified in its incident-response engagements occurred on May 27, 2023, four days before Progress publicly announced the vulnerability on May 31. Exploitation involved SQL-injection activity directed at the legitimate `guestaccess.aspx` endpoint, followed by deployment of the LEMURLOOT web shell, usually disguised as a legitimate MOVEit component using filenames such as `human.aspx`, `human2.aspx`, or `_human2.aspx` ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

LEMURLOOT was purpose-built for MOVEit Transfer. It could enumerate files and folders, retrieve application and database information, extract Azure Blob Storage settings, download files, and create or delete a user account using the hard-coded name “Health Check Service.” Mandiant observed instances in which data theft occurred within minutes of web-shell deployment and reported the theft of large volumes of files from multiple victims ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

Mandiant initially tracked the activity as UNC4857. On June 6, 2023, it merged UNC4857 into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and data-leak-site overlaps. The same reporting connects the campaign to the CL0P^_-LEAKS data-leak site, where a June 6 post claimed responsibility and threatened victims with publication of stolen data unless they paid an extortion fee ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)). The strongest supported conclusion is therefore that the MOVEit exploitation campaign was a FIN11-attributed mass exploitation and data-theft operation associated with the CL0P extortion brand or ecosystem. The source evidence supports the attribution as a Mandiant assessment, not as an independently adjudicated fact.

## Scope and Source Assessment

This report uses two distinct source records:

| Source ID | Source | Role in analysis |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Mandiant, “Zero-Day Vulnerability in MOVEit Transfer Exploited for Data Theft,” dated June 2, 2023, reproduced through the CISA advisory URL | Intrusion chronology, LEMURLOOT behavior, infrastructure, attribution, and extortion activity |
| S2 | NIST National Vulnerability Database, CVE-2023-34362 detail page | Vulnerability description, severity, affected-product information, CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities status, and change history |

S1 is the primary source for the campaign investigation because it describes observations from Mandiant incident-response engagements, malware analysis, infrastructure analysis, and attribution work. S2 is the authoritative vulnerability-record source for the CVE description, severity, affected configurations, and catalog status. The supplied material duplicates both source records; duplicates are treated as one source each.

## Vulnerability Disclosure and Exploitation Timeline

### Pre-disclosure exploitation

The campaign’s operational activity predates public disclosure. Mandiant states that the earliest evidence of exploitation observed through its incident-response engagements occurred on May 27, 2023. The activity resulted in web-shell deployment and data theft, with theft sometimes occurring within minutes of deployment ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

Progress Software announced the vulnerability on May 31, 2023, assigning it CVE-2023-34362. The chronology therefore shows exploitation of the zero-day before the vendor announcement and before the vulnerability was publicly documented in the NVD. This sequencing is significant because it demonstrates that defenders could have been exposed during a period when ordinary vulnerability-management processes had no public CVE record to prioritize ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a); [S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)).

### Public CVE record and severity

The NVD describes CVE-2023-34362 as a SQL-injection vulnerability in MOVEit Transfer that allowed an unauthenticated attacker to gain access to the product’s database. Depending on whether the deployment used MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, or Azure SQL, an attacker could infer database structure and contents or execute SQL statements that altered or deleted database elements ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)).

The NVD records the following CVSS v3.1 characteristics:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Attack vector | Network |
| Attack complexity | Low |
| Privileges required | None |
| User interaction | None |
| Scope | Unchanged |
| Confidentiality impact | High |
| Integrity impact | High |
| Availability impact | High |
| Base score | 9.8 — Critical |

These values describe a vulnerability that is remotely exploitable without authentication or user interaction and that can affect confidentiality, integrity, and availability ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)).

The NVD also identifies CWE-89, “Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (‘SQL Injection’),” and records that the CVE was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on June 2, 2023. The catalog action was to apply updates according to vendor instructions, with a listed federal deadline of June 23, 2023 ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)).

## Affected Versions and Remediation Context

The NVD record identifies affected MOVEit Transfer and MOVEit Cloud versions. The supplied record contains both the original public description and later expanded configuration data. The principal affected ranges shown in the record are:

| Product | Affected versions shown in S2 | Fixed threshold shown in S2 |
|---|---|---|
| MOVEit Transfer 2020.1 | Up to and including 2020.1.6 | Later CPE data identifies versions up to 2020.1.6 as affected |
| MOVEit Transfer 2021.0 | Before 2021.0.7 in later CPE data | 2021.0.7 |
| MOVEit Transfer 2021.1 | Before 2021.1.5 in later CPE data | 2021.1.5 |
| MOVEit Transfer 2022.0 | Before 2022.0.5 in later CPE data | 2022.0.5 |
| MOVEit Transfer 2022.1 | Before 2022.1.6 in later CPE data | 2022.1.6 |
| MOVEit Transfer 2023.0 | Before 2023.0.2 in later CPE data | 2023.0.2 |
| MOVEit Cloud | Multiple affected ranges, including versions below 14.0.5.45, 14.1.6.97, and 15.0.2.39 | Corresponding thresholds in later CPE data |

The original NVD description lists earlier fixed versions—such as 2021.0.6, 2021.1.4, 2022.0.4, 2022.1.5, and 2023.0.1—while later CPE data in the same record shows different affected thresholds. This should be treated as a record-history issue rather than silently reconciled. Organizations should rely on the vendor’s current remediation guidance rather than the older description alone ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362)).

## Exploitation Chain

### Initial access through SQL injection

Mandiant observed multiple POST requests to the legitimate `guestaccess.aspx` file before interaction with the malicious web shell. It assessed that this pattern indicated SQL-injection attacks were directed at that endpoint ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

The vulnerability’s unauthenticated nature allowed the attackers to reach the application remotely without valid credentials. The supplied evidence does not establish a single exploit payload, exact SQL statements used during initial exploitation, or whether every victim experienced identical request sequences. It does, however, support the assessment that exploitation of `guestaccess.aspx` preceded LEMURLOOT deployment in observed cases.

### Web-shell deployment

Following exploitation, the actors deployed LEMURLOOT, a newly identified web shell written in C# and tailored specifically to MOVEit Transfer. The malware used filenames that masqueraded as legitimate MOVEit files, including `human.aspx`, `human2.aspx`, and `_human2.aspx`. Several `human2.aspx` samples were uploaded to VirusTotal beginning May 28, 2023, although the source does not establish that every upload represented a distinct victim or attacker action ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

The masquerading strategy was operationally important because it placed malicious ASP.NET content alongside or under the appearance of a legitimate MOVEit component. Mandiant supplied YARA rules intended to hunt for both compiled LEMURLOOT DLLs and ASP.NET scripts. Those rules reference strings such as `X-siLock-Comment`, `X-siLock-Step2`, `X-siLock-Step3`, and “Health Check Service.” Mandiant expressly warned that the rules were hunting starting points and had not been tested as production blocking rules ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

### LEMURLOOT authentication and command handling

LEMURLOOT authenticated incoming connections using a hard-coded password represented by a 36-character GUID-formatted value. It expected the `X-siLock-Comment` HTTP header. Requests failing the expected header-and-value check received an HTTP 404 response. A successful connection caused the shell to return an `X-siLock-Comment` response header with the value `comment` ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

The shell processed commands from three HTTP headers:

- `X-siLock-Step1`
- `X-siLock-Step2`
- `X-siLock-Step3`

The reported functions were:

| Function | Reported behavior |
|---|---|
| System and storage discovery | Retrieves MOVEit Azure storage settings, including account, key, and container information |
| File and folder enumeration | Queries information about files, file sizes, folders, file owners, and institution names |
| File theft | Retrieves files by file and folder identifiers and returns them compressed |
| Account manipulation | Creates an account using “Health Check Service” values or locates an existing account with permission level 30 |
| Cleanup | Deletes a user account whose real name is “Health Check Service” |
| Data transfer | Returns data to the operator in gzip-compressed form |

These capabilities show that LEMURLOOT was not a generic web shell merely providing command execution. It was designed to understand MOVEit’s application data and file-management model, thereby supporting structured discovery and targeted or bulk theft ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

## Data Theft and Cloud Storage Exposure

Mandiant reported multiple cases involving large volumes of files stolen from MOVEit Transfer systems. It assessed that the web shell was used to steal files previously uploaded by users of individual MOVEit systems ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

LEMURLOOT could also retrieve Azure Blob Storage information from MOVEit application settings, including the configured storage account, associated key, and container. This created a potential secondary exposure for victims storing appliance data in Azure Blob Storage. The source is careful not to state that all Azure data was stolen or that theft was limited to Azure-hosted data. The supported conclusion is narrower: the malware had the capability to obtain Azure storage configuration and credentials, and this capability could have enabled access to relevant cloud-hosted files in some deployments ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

## Infrastructure and Operational Pattern

Mandiant observed scanning and exploitation from IP addresses in the `5.252.188.0/22` range in many cases. It also noted that web-shell interaction and data theft came from different systems, indicating separation between initial exploitation infrastructure and later operational infrastructure ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

Many systems used for second-stage operations hosted RDP services with certificates generated between May 19 and May 22, 2023. Mandiant assessed that these certificate dates were suggestive of infrastructure staging. This is an analytical indicator, not proof that every system was staged on those dates or that certificate creation alone identifies the operators ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

Mandiant also identified overlaps in internet service providers, network blocks, and IP addresses between the MOVEit campaign and historical FIN11 activity. One IP address attempting exploitation of CVE-2023-34362 had reportedly been used by FIN11 as early as mid-January 2023. The same system had hosted RDP on TCP port 3389 and continued presenting the same X.509 certificate when later used in the MOVEit activity ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

## Attribution to FIN11 and CL0P-Linked Extortion

Mandiant initially attributed the activity to UNC4857. On June 6, 2023, it merged UNC4857 into FIN11 based on four categories of overlap: targeting, infrastructure, certificates, and the data-leak site ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

The campaign’s extortion linkage developed publicly in stages:

1. Mandiant initially observed data theft without immediate ransom demands.
2. On June 5, Bleeping Computer reported that an individual described as affiliated with the CLOP ransomware group claimed responsibility for incidents involving exploitation of the MOVEit vulnerability.
3. On June 6, a post on the `CL0P^_-LEAKS` data-leak site claimed responsibility and threatened to publish stolen data unless victims paid an extortion fee.
4. Mandiant linked the activity to FIN11 based on the overlap evidence described above ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

Mandiant characterized the campaign as consistent with prior FIN11-attributed data-theft extortion involving other file-transfer products, including Accellion’s legacy File Transfer Appliance and GoAnywhere MFT. These comparisons support behavioral continuity, but they do not independently prove that every actor, server, or tool in those earlier campaigns was identical to those in the MOVEit campaign ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

The evidence does not show that Mandiant directly observed extortion emails sent to confirmed victims at the time of publication. Mandiant stated that previous FIN11 operations sometimes delayed ransom communications for several weeks, and it assessed that a similar delay was plausible in this campaign. That explanation is explicitly an assessment and should not be treated as a confirmed operational fact ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a)).

## Overall Assessment

The evidence supports a coherent exploitation sequence: a pre-disclosure SQL-injection campaign against exposed MOVEit Transfer systems; deployment of the MOVEit-specific LEMURLOOT web shell; rapid enumeration and theft of locally stored files and potentially Azure Blob-hosted data; and later public association with the CL0P^_-LEAKS extortion site. Mandiant’s subsequent merger of UNC4857 into FIN11 is supported by infrastructure, certificate, targeting, and data-leak-site overlaps.

My concrete assessment is that the MOVEit incident was not merely a vulnerability-disclosure event or isolated exploitation. It was a scalable, opportunistic data-theft campaign using a specialized post-exploitation implant and infrastructure that Mandiant assessed as FIN11-linked, with public extortion activity tied to the CL0P brand. The attribution is well supported within the supplied evidence but remains an intelligence assessment rather than a judicially established identity determination.

This blog post has been updated to reflect the new attribution and supporting evidence. Mandiant has observed wide exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer secure managed file transfer software for subsequent data theft. This vulnerability was announced by Progress Software Corporation on May 31, 2023 and has been assigned CVE-2023-34362. Based on initial analysis from Mandiant incident response engagements, the earliest evidence of exploitation occurred on May 27, 2023 resulting in deployment of web shells and data theft. In some instances, data theft has occurred within minutes of the deployment of web shells. The seemingly opportunistic nature of this campaign and the subsequent data theft is consistent with activity we’ve seen from extortion actors; however, victims did not initially receive any ransom demands. Then on June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site (DLS) claimed responsibility for this activity and threatened to post stolen data if victims did not pay an extortion fee. Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and DLS overlaps. This campaign has impacted organizations operating in a wide range of industries based in Canada, India, and the U.S., but the impact is almost certainly broader than Mandiant has directly observed. Following exploitation of the vulnerability, the threat actors are deploying a newly discovered LEMURLOOT web shell with filenames that masquerade as human.aspx, which is a legitimate component of the MOVEit Transfer software. Mandiant has observed several POST requests made to the legitimate guestaccess.aspx file before interaction with the LEMURLOOT webshell, indicating SQL injection attacks were directed towards that file. We have observed LEMURLOOT samples with the filenames human2.aspx and _human2.aspx. Various samples with the name human2.aspx were uploaded to VirusTotal beginning on May 28, 2023. Samples of LEMURLOOT have been uploaded to public repositories from several additional countries—including Italy, Pakistan, and Germany—suggesting that UNC4857 has also impacted organizations in these nations. LEMURLOOT provides functionality tailored to execute on a system running MOVEit Transfer software, including the ability to generate commands to enumerate files and folders, retrieve configuration information, and create or delete a user with a hard-coded name. Initial analysis suggests that the LEMURLOOT web shell is being used to steal data previously uploaded by the users of individual MOVEit Transfer systems. Mandiant is aware of multiple cases where large volumes of files have been stolen from victims' MOVEit transfer systems. LEMURLOOT can also steal Azure Storage Blob information, including credentials, from the MOVEit Transfer application settings, suggesting that actors exploiting this vulnerability may be stealing files from Azure in cases where victims are storing appliance data in Azure Blob storage, although it is unclear if theft is limited to data stored in this way. In many cases, the scanning and exploitation leading to the delivery of LEMURLOOT was sourced from IP addresses in the range 5.252.188.0/22, however interaction with the web shell and data theft came from different systems. Many of the hosts used to support these second-stage operations hosted RDP services with certificates generated between May 19 and 22, which is suggestive of when this infrastructure may have been staged. Analysis of this intrusion activity is ongoing and will be reflected on the CAMP.23.037 page within Mandiant Advantage; we will also update this blog post if and when additional information becomes available. Along with this blog post, Mandiant has produced a detailed MOVEit Containment and Hardening guide to assist organizations with this event. The document contains guidance on the following key items: Containment Measures Application and Infrastructure Hardening Logging and Hunting Recommendations LEMURLOOT Analysis LEMURLOOT is a web shell written in C# tailored to interact with the MOVEit Transfer platform. The malware authenticates incoming connections via a hard-coded password and can run commands that will download files from the MOVEit Transfer system, extract its Azure system settings, retrieve detailed record information, create and insert a particular user, or delete this same user. Data returned to the system interacting with LEMURLOOT is gzip compressed. Authentication and Database Connection LEMURLOOT first checks if an incoming HTTP request contains the header field X-siLock-Comment and a corresponding 36-character GUID-formatted value, which varies across samples. It effectively uses this GUID as a password and returns an HTTP 404 status code to clients that do not pass the expected header field and value. If the correct password is passed to LEMURLOOT, it sends a header response X-siLock-Comment and value comment, indicating the connection is successful and can accept tasking. The malware connects to a SQL server from the executing host using the settings retrieved using SystemSettings.DatabaseSettings(). It then processes data received from the connecting client, parsing expected commands from the following HTTP header fields: X-siLock-Step1, X-siLock-Step2, and X-siLock-Step3. X-siLock-Step1 Command Sequence If the value of the header field X-siLock-Step1 is -1, LEMURLOOT retrieves and returns the Azure system settings from MOVEit Transfer, including the configured Azure Blog storage account, and its associated key and container (AzureBlobStorageAccount, AzureBlobKey, and AzureBlobContainer). It then performs SQL queries to retrieve files, file size, folders, file owners, and institution name data. The resulting data is gzip compressed and returned to the client interacting with LEMURLOOT. If the X-siLock-Step1 header field value is -2, it deletes a user account with the LoginName and RealName set to "Health Check Service" using the SQL command in Figure 1. Note that this user is inserted using the following functionality. Delete FROM users WHERE RealName='Health Check Service' Figure 1: MOVEit user deletion command X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 Command Sequence If the value of header field X-siLock-Step1 is neither -1 or -2, the malware parses the values from header fields X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 and stores them in variables named fileid and folderid, respectively. If the values of fileid and folderid are not null, the malware retrieves the file from the local MOVEit Transfer system with these same values, gzip compresses it, and returns it to the connecting client. If the fileid and folderid variables are null, LEMURLOOT attempts to identify an existing account with permission level “30” and InstID = the value set from "X-siLock-Step1" otherwise it creates a new account with a randomly generated username and with LoginName and RealName values set to "Health Check Service" This account is inserted it into an active MOVEit application session. Attribution Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and data leak site (DLS) overlaps. The activity is reminiscent of prior mass exploitation events targeting file transfer software and leading to FIN11-attributed data theft extortion via the CL0P^_- LEAKS data leak site (DLS). FIN11-attributed data theft extortion has occurred following exploitation of multiple other file transfer systems. From late 2020 to early 2021, threat actors exploited multiple zero-day vulnerabilities in Accellion's legacy File Transfer Appliance (FTA) to install the DEWMODE web shell. Similarly, in early 2023, threat actors exploited GoAnywhere Managed File Transfer (MFT) vulnerability CVE-2023-0669. Mandiant has identified numerous overlaps in the ISPs, netblocks, and IP addresses used in this campaign and historical FIN11 operations. Notably, an IP address that was attempting exploitation of CVE-2023-34362 was used by FIN11 as early as mid-January 2023. At the time this system was first used by FIN11 it was hosting an RDP service on TCP port 3389. This service was still active and presenting the same x509 certificate when UNC4857's use of the system began. On June 5, 2023, Bleeping Computer claimed that someone affiliated with the CLOP ransomware group stated that they were behind incidents in which the MOVEit transfer system vulnerability was exploited for data theft. On June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS claimed responsibility for this activity (Figure 2). Figure 2: CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS post Implications Mandiant routinely observes threat actors with varying motivations targeting sensitive data. For example, state-sponsored threat actors have demonstrated ongoing interest in targeting entities with policy research, military and government files, intellectual property, and personally identifiable information. Cyber criminals can also directly monetize stolen data via extortion operations, post it for sale on underground forums, or leverage it in secondary operations such as business email compromise. Mandiant has not yet directly observed any extortion emails sent to confirmed victims. However, in prior cases where FIN11 exploited vulnerabilities in secure file transfer systems, the threat actors did not send extortion emails demanding a payment in return for not publishing the data on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS until several weeks later. It is plausible that FIN11 delayed sending the ransom emails in an attempt to extend the amount of time that the zero-day vulnerabilities remained undetected and thus increase the number of victims and/or capacity to negotiate with a large number of victims simultaneously. Although the CLOP brand has posted to their DLS suggesting victims should initiate contact, if their TTPs remain consistent it is likely that the group will begin to initiate contact with some impacted organizations in the coming days and/or weeks. This blog post has been updated to reflect the new attribution and supporting evidence. Mandiant has observed wide exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer secure managed file transfer software for subsequent data theft. This vulnerability was announced by Progress Software Corporation on May 31, 2023 and has been assigned CVE-2023-34362. Based on initial analysis from Mandiant incident response engagements, the earliest evidence of exploitation occurred on May 27, 2023 resulting in deployment of web shells and data theft. In some instances, data theft has occurred within minutes of the deployment of web shells. The seemingly opportunistic nature of this campaign and the subsequent data theft is consistent with activity we’ve seen from extortion actors; however, victims did not initially receive any ransom demands. Then on June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site (DLS) claimed responsibility for this activity and threatened to post stolen data if victims did not pay an extortion fee. Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and DLS overlaps. This campaign has impacted organizations operating in a wide range of industries based in Canada, India, and the U.S., but the impact is almost certainly broader than Mandiant has directly observed. Following exploitation of the vulnerability, the threat actors are deploying a newly discovered LEMURLOOT web shell with filenames that masquerade as human.aspx, which is a legitimate component of the MOVEit Transfer software. Mandiant has observed several POST requests made to the legitimate guestaccess.aspx file before interaction with the LEMURLOOT webshell, indicating SQL injection attacks were directed towards that file. We have observed LEMURLOOT samples with the filenames human2.aspx and _human2.aspx. Various samples with the name human2.aspx were uploaded to VirusTotal beginning on May 28, 2023. Samples of LEMURLOOT have been uploaded to public repositories from several additional countries—including Italy, Pakistan, and Germany—suggesting that UNC4857 has also impacted organizations in these nations. LEMURLOOT provides functionality tailored to execute on a system running MOVEit Transfer software, including the ability to generate commands to enumerate files and folders, retrieve configuration information, and create or delete a user with a hard-coded name. Initial analysis suggests that the LEMURLOOT web shell is being used to steal data previously uploaded by the users of individual MOVEit Transfer systems. Mandiant is aware of multiple cases where large volumes of files have been stolen from victims' MOVEit transfer systems. LEMURLOOT can also steal Azure Storage Blob information, including credentials, from the MOVEit Transfer application settings, suggesting that actors exploiting this vulnerability may be stealing files from Azure in cases where victims are storing appliance data in Azure Blob storage, although it is unclear if theft is limited to data stored in this way. In many cases, the scanning and exploitation leading to the delivery of LEMURLOOT was sourced from IP addresses in the range 5.252.188.0/22, however interaction with the web shell and data theft came from different systems. Many of the hosts used to support these second-stage operations hosted RDP services with certificates generated between May 19 and 22, which is suggestive of when this infrastructure may have been staged. Analysis of this intrusion activity is ongoing and will be reflected on the CAMP.23.037 page within Mandiant Advantage; we will also update this blog post if and when additional information becomes available. Along with this blog post, Mandiant has produced a detailed MOVEit Containment and Hardening guide to assist organizations with this event. The document contains guidance on the following key items: Containment Measures Application and Infrastructure Hardening Logging and Hunting Recommendations LEMURLOOT Analysis LEMURLOOT is a web shell written in C# tailored to interact with the MOVEit Transfer platform. The malware authenticates incoming connections via a hard-coded password and can run commands that will download files from the MOVEit Transfer system, extract its Azure system settings, retrieve detailed record information, create and insert a particular user, or delete this same user. Data returned to the system interacting with LEMURLOOT is gzip compressed. Authentication and Database Connection LEMURLOOT first checks if an incoming HTTP request contains the header field X-siLock-Comment and a corresponding 36-character GUID-formatted value, which varies across samples. It effectively uses this GUID as a password and returns an HTTP 404 status code to clients that do not pass the expected header field and value. If the correct password is passed to LEMURLOOT, it sends a header response X-siLock-Comment and value comment, indicating the connection is successful and can accept tasking. The malware connects to a SQL server from the executing host using the settings retrieved using SystemSettings.DatabaseSettings(). It then processes data received from the connecting client, parsing expected commands from the following HTTP header fields: X-siLock-Step1, X-siLock-Step2, and X-siLock-Step3. X-siLock-Step1 Command Sequence If the value of the header field X-siLock-Step1 is -1, LEMURLOOT retrieves and returns the Azure system settings from MOVEit Transfer, including the configured Azure Blog storage account, and its associated key and container (AzureBlobStorageAccount, AzureBlobKey, and AzureBlobContainer). It then performs SQL queries to retrieve files, file size, folders, file owners, and institution name data. The resulting data is gzip compressed and returned to the client interacting with LEMURLOOT. If the X-siLock-Step1 header field value is -2, it deletes a user account with the LoginName and RealName set to "Health Check Service" using the SQL command in Figure 1. Note that this user is inserted using the following functionality. Delete FROM users WHERE RealName='Health Check Service' Figure 1: MOVEit user deletion command X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 Command Sequence If the value of header field X-siLock-Step1 is neither -1 or -2, the malware parses the values from header fields X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 and stores them in variables named fileid and folderid, respectively. If the values of fileid and folderid are not null, the malware retrieves the file from the local MOVEit Transfer system with these same values, gzip compresses it, and returns it to the connecting client. If the fileid and folderid variables are null, LEMURLOOT attempts to identify an existing account with permission level “30” and InstID = the value set from "X-siLock-Step1" otherwise it creates a new account with a randomly generated username and with LoginName and RealName values set to "Health Check Service" This account is inserted it into an active MOVEit application session. Attribution Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and data leak site (DLS) overlaps. The activity is reminiscent of prior mass exploitation events targeting file transfer software and leading to FIN11-attributed data theft extortion via the CL0P^_- LEAKS data leak site (DLS). FIN11-attributed data theft extortion has occurred following exploitation of multiple other file transfer systems. From late 2020 to early 2021, threat actors exploited multiple zero-day vulnerabilities in Accellion's legacy File Transfer Appliance (FTA) to install the DEWMODE web shell. Similarly, in early 2023, threat actors exploited GoAnywhere Managed File Transfer (MFT) vulnerability CVE-2023-0669. Mandiant has identified numerous overlaps in the ISPs, netblocks, and IP addresses used in this campaign and historical FIN11 operations. Notably, an IP address that was attempting exploitation of CVE-2023-34362 was used by FIN11 as early as mid-January 2023. At the time this system was first used by FIN11 it was hosting an RDP service on TCP port 3389. This service was still active and presenting the same x509 certificate when UNC4857's use of the system began. On June 5, 2023, Bleeping Computer claimed that someone affiliated with the CLOP ransomware group stated that they were behind incidents in which the MOVEit transfer system vulnerability was exploited for data theft. On June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS claimed responsibility for this activity (Figure 2). Figure 2: CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS post Implications Mandiant routinely observes threat actors with varying motivations targeting sensitive data. For example, state-sponsored threat actors have demonstrated ongoing interest in targeting entities with policy research, military and government files, intellectual property, and personally identifiable information. Cyber criminals can also directly monetize stolen data via extortion operations, post it for sale on underground forums, or leverage it in secondary operations such as business email compromise. Mandiant has not yet directly observed any extortion emails sent to confirmed victims. However, in prior cases where FIN11 exploited vulnerabilities in secure file transfer systems, the threat actors did not send extortion emails demanding a payment in return for not publishing the data on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS until several weeks later. It is plausible that FIN11 delayed sending the ransom emails in an attempt to extend the amount of time that the zero-day vulnerabilities remained undetected and thus increase the number of victims and/or capacity to negotiate with a large number of victims simultaneously. Although the CLOP brand has posted to their DLS suggesting victims should initiate contact, if their TTPs remain consistent it is likely that the group will begin to initiate contact with some impacted organizations in the coming days and/or weeks.
